transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, thank you, doctor. It's... it's really my sleep that's the issue, which is highly unusual for me. I am, or at least I have always been, an incredibly disciplined sleeper. You really have to be, in my position—I'm a chief executive, so my schedule is usually managed down to the minute, and I've always treated my sleep with that exact same level of rigor. Seven hours, lights out, no exceptions. 

But lately... well, ever since my cousin passed away, that entire structure has just completely collapsed. I get into bed, and instead of winding down, I just lie there, wide awake, completely unable to shut my brain off. I just keep replaying that night over and over in my head. And then, when I finally do manage to drift off from sheer exhaustion, it doesn't last. I'll jolt awake at 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning, and my mind is just filled with these... these awful scraps of images from the hospital. Just flashes of it, really, but enough to completely ruin the rest of the night. So by the time morning rolls around, I'm dragging myself into these high-stakes board meetings feeling like I’ve only slept in pieces. It's completely unsustainable, and frankly, I just need to get back to my normal routine because I cannot function like this.
When you're lying in bed unable to sleep, are these thoughts about your cousin's passing something that keeps coming back to you, even when you don't want them to?

Yes, exactly. I absolutely do not want them there. It is incredibly frustrating because, as I've mentioned, I am very accustomed to controlling my environment, my schedule, and certainly my own thoughts. I'll be lying there, actively trying to focus on something productive—maybe running through the next day's agenda or just focusing on my breathing—and the memories just force their way in anyway. 

But honestly, doctor, it's... it's not even just when I'm in bed trying to sleep. That might actually be the most unsettling part of all of this. It happens at the most odd, unpredictable moments during the day, too. For instance, if I hear a phone ring late in the evening, or even just... if I'm driving and I catch the sudden glare of headlights coming down the highway. It's like a trigger I didn't ask for. Suddenly, this incredibly sharp picture of the hospital corridor just pushes its way right into my mind. It's so vivid. And it's not just visual, either—I can hear the police officer’s voice, the exact tone he used, just cutting through whatever I'm actually trying to focus on. 

It hits me so suddenly that I literally have to stop what I'm doing. I have to physically pause, take a deep breath, and just steady myself before I can even think about resuming my day. And in my line of work, you simply cannot afford to freeze up or lose your train of thought, but these... these flashes, they don't care what I'm doing or who I'm meeting with. They just barge right in completely uninvited.
Since your cousin passed away, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities that remind you of what happened, or feeling emotionally numb in ways you didn’t before?

Well, as for avoiding things, I wouldn't say I'm actively avoiding places or people. I mean, my schedule simply doesn't allow for me to just drop off the map, so I am still attending all the necessary functions and keeping my appointments. I have to. But the emotional part... that is something I have noticed, and it's quite disturbing, honestly. 

It's not exactly numbness, but more of a... a complete absence of the positive feelings I should be having, if that makes sense. For example, my family has had several prayer gatherings since he passed. We're quite a close-knit extended family, usually, and these gatherings are meant to be a source of comfort. And I go, of course I go. I dress appropriately, I say all the right things, I thank everyone for their condolences. I go through all the motions perfectly. But inside... inside, it's just completely blank. 

Even when my nieces—who I adore, absolutely adore—even when they came over to my house the other evening. They brought dinner, they were trying so hard to be supportive and comforting, hugging me and telling me they loved me. And normally, I would feel such warmth from that, such a deep sense of connection and gratitude for them. But I just sat there, behaving properly, thanking them, and feeling absolutely nothing. No warmth, no relief, no comfort whatsoever. It was as if that entire affectionate, loving part of my brain had just been switched off, or gone completely quiet. It's incredibly disconcerting because I know I love them, I know I should be feeling comforted by their presence, but there's just this... this void where those positive emotions are supposed to be. It makes me feel almost robotic, just going through the motions of being a grieving family member without actually feeling any of the love or support that's being offered to me.

Outside of these family gatherings and interactions with your nieces, have you noticed this same lack of positive emotion in other areas of your life—like at work, during hobbies, or when interacting with friends?

Well, as I was just explaining... it's really most pronounced with my family. I mean, I was just saying how during those prayer gatherings, and even when my nieces came over to comfort me—which was incredibly sweet of them, they really went out of their way—I found myself just behaving properly, saying the right things, but feeling absolutely no warmth or relief inside. It's almost as if that affectionate, positive part of me has just gone completely quiet. 

At work, though? Work is... well, work is different. I wouldn't say I expect to feel "warmth" at the office, you know? It's a high-pressure environment, I'm a chief executive, I have a board to report to, shareholders to keep happy. The emotions I experience there are usually driven by adrenaline, focus, maybe a bit of frustration when things don't go according to plan. So I haven't really noticed a lack of positive emotion there, because the baseline is just so different. I'm still driven, I still want to succeed, even if I'm exhausted. 

As for hobbies... frankly, doctor, I don't really have time for hobbies right now. Between the insomnia, trying to keep the company running, and dealing with all the family matters surrounding my cousin's estate—because of course, I'm the one everyone looks to for organizing these things—there simply isn't a spare moment in the day. And friends? My friends are mostly colleagues or people in my professional network. We meet for dinner, we discuss the market, we talk about our portfolios. It's very cordial, very pleasant, but again, it's not the kind of deep, emotional connection where I would notice this... this void I was telling you about. 

It really is just with my family, where I *should* be feeling that deep love and comfort, that I notice this complete blankness. Like with my nieces, as I said. They were hugging me, and I just felt... nothing. Just going through the motions. It's very strange, and as I said, quite disconcerting.

The persistence and specificity of the trauma-related symptoms, along with re-experiencing and emotional detachment, support this narrowing.
